marble.name: Pushes & Pulls
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Understand that pushes and pulls are forces that can change the speed or direction of an object's motion, and compare the effects of different strengths and directions
marble.prompt: Can you explain that pushing a toy car harder makes it go faster, and pushing it sideways makes it change direction?

cluster.summary: Your child is learning about forces — understanding how pushes and pulls can make objects move faster, slower, or change direction, and testing different ways to affect motion.

misconceptions: Only living/animate things can push or pull (a table or wall can't exert a force).
There is only a force if you can see movement — a push that doesn't visibly move something 'isn't a force'.
Impetus seed: a moving object has 'force' or 'go' stored inside it that gradually runs out, which is why it stops (MOSART; RESPeCT Grade 3).
Force is the same as the object's energy / a property the object owns, rather than an interaction between two objects.
A bigger push makes something go faster and faster forever (constant push → ever-increasing or fixed speed confusion, in seed form).
representations: Real manipulable objects (the primary 'representation' at this age — balls, cars, trolleys)
Simple direction arrows showing which way the push/pull acts (seed of the force-arrow representation)
Before/after motion pictures (object at rest → moving; fast → slow)
authoredAnswer: Give it a hard/strong push in my direction. A stronger push makes it speed up more, so a hard push makes it go faster than a gentle one; the push is the force that starts it moving and sets how fast it goes.
probe: Give one ball the same push on a smooth floor and on a rough carpet. Before rolling, ask the child to predict which travels further and WHY. Many predict 'the same, because I pushed the same' or 'it stops when the push runs out'; seeing the carpet ball stop sooner sets up friction (the ground rubbing) as the cause rath

wrongAnswers.wrong: It doesn't matter how hard you push — the ball rolls the same either way.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: In tier 2 the child cannot say a stronger push gives more speed; treats every push as equivalent.
wrongAnswers.fix: Line up two identical balls, tap one gently and shove the other, and race them so the child SEES strength map to speed, then name it.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Explains continued motion by a force stored in the ball rather than the hand's push having ended.
wrongAnswers.fix: Don't teach formal inertia; point to the floor/carpet rubbing (friction) as what slows it, and revisit on a slippery vs rough floor. Expect this idea to return and challenge it repeatedly.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: When asked to slow or steer a rolling ball, says you can only stop it by grabbing it, or that a push can't change direction.
wrongAnswers.fix: Demonstrate a cushion pushing against a rolling ball (slowing) and a sideways tap (turning); name both as the push changing the motion.
